about: Spoken commentary for the universe film (public/universe/), written to be heard: a narrator telling the story to a beginner. The lines of each scene play one after another with short pauses; while narration is on, the film slows each scene just enough for its lines (universe.js, narrPlan). Every claim follows the scene cards and their sources. tools/narration.py records the files (engine 'say' or 'elevenlabs') and fills in 'dur' (seconds).

cues.text: Let's go back to the very beginning, about thirteen point eight billion years ago.
Some scientists think that, right at the start, even space and time didn't exist the way we know them.
Honestly, nobody's sure what happened here. This is the very edge of what science can explain.
Then, in far less than the blink of an eye, space itself may have stretched, enormously.
Imagine dots drawn on a balloon. As you blow it up, every dot moves away from every other.
Watch these three gaps: they grow together, just like that.
And then, as suddenly as it began, the stretching stops.
What's left is unimaginably hot, far hotter than the centre of any star.
Everything is a boiling soup of tiny particles called quarks, zipping around freely.
But the universe is cooling fast. Within about ten millionths of a second, the quarks huddle together in threes.
They form protons and neutrons, the building blocks of every atom.
About three minutes in, the whole universe works like a giant nuclear furnace.
Protons and neutrons slam together and stick. Every flash you see is a new helium nucleus being born.
By around twenty minutes, it's all over.
The mix is set: about three quarters hydrogen and one quarter helium, the same mix we still find in the oldest clouds of gas today.
For the next three hundred and eighty thousand years, space is filled with a glowing fog, so thick that light can't get through.
Then it cools enough for atoms to form, and the fog finally clears.
Light streams out in every direction, for the very first time.
And here's the amazing part: that same ancient light is still reaching us today, from every direction in the sky.
After that comes a long, dark stretch. There are no stars yet, nothing shining at all.
But in the darkness, gravity is busy.
It slowly pulls gas, and invisible dark matter, into long strands and clumps, like a giant cosmic spider web.
About two hundred million years in, where those strands meet, the first stars switch on.
They were probably giants, much bigger than our Sun, and they burned out in just a few million years.
When they exploded, they made the first carbon, oxygen and iron.
That was the start of the atoms that, much later, would build planets, and people like you.
Next, stars gather into galaxies, and their light clears away the haze around them, bubble by bubble.
The James Webb Space Telescope has actually seen galaxies this old.
And one young galaxy, just like these, would grow up to become our own.
Billions of years pass, and our galaxy, the Milky Way, keeps growing.
It makes new stars, and it swallows smaller galaxies that wander too close.
That faint trail of stars is one of them, still on the move today.
And the dashed ring shows where our Sun travels around the galaxy now.
Finally, about four and a half billion years ago, a cloud of gas and dust collapses, and right at its centre, our Sun is born.
Around it, a spinning disc of dust slowly clumps into pebbles, then rocks, then whole planets.
One of them is the Earth: hot, glowing and molten, and still being hit by leftover rock.
And that's where our home's own story begins.
